item.title: The Creality K2 SE 4C 3D Printer gives you four-color printing for $359
item.itunes:title: The Creality K2 SE 4C 3D Printer gives you four-color printing for $359
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If you've been eyeing a 3D printer that can print in more than one color, the Creality K2 SE 4C is worth a look. Amazon has this versatile 3D printer down to $359, a 23% savings and a solid discount on a multicolor machine rated for speeds up to 500mm/s.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover
Creality K2 SE 4C
Build Volume
220 × 215 × 245 mm
Printing Speed
500 mm/s
Connectivity
USB drive, 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi

The Creality K2 SE 4C is a compact CoreXY multicolor FDM 3D printer with four built-in filament slots that uses 37% less space than the K2 SE Combo. It prints at up to 500 mm/s, with a 220 × 215 × 245 mm build volume and full-auto bed leveling.

See at Amazon

Save 23% on the Creality K2 SE 4C

Four colors for a lot of versatility

The 4C in the name Creality K2 SE 4C stands for four colors, fed from an open four-spool rack on the side of the frame into one hotend. It doesn't blend colors, but with all four spools loaded, you can switch colors within a single print. Creality rates the printer for speeds up to 500 mm/s and acceleration up to 20,000 mm/s², though it says 300 mm/s is the speed for optimal surface quality, so think of 500 mm/s as the ceiling.

When it comes to the hardware, you're looking at a 220 by 215 by 245mm print volume, a dual-gear direct-drive extruder, an epoxy resin build plate, and a heated bed that reaches up to 100°C. Layer heights run from 0.1 to 0.35mm on 1.75mm filament, and Creality lists PLA, PETG, and PLA-CF as compatible. Smart leveling probes only the print area.

As for programming the printing, you'll work from a 3.97-inch color touchscreen with 2.4GHz Wi-Fi, USB file transfer, and 8GB of eMMC storage. Creality also has Power Loss Recovery, run-out and tangle detection, Skip Partial Failure, and Auto Filament Relay. The Creality K2 SE 4C is, as a result, pretty beginner-friendly, as it'll help with a lot of the common errors you'll come across.

The 500 mm/s rating, four-color setup, and $110.99 in savings make the Creality K2 SE 4C an easy pick if you want to try multicolor prints. Grab it on Amazon while it's still on sale.

item.title: The Fanttik S1 Pro electric screwdriver with three torque settings drops to $40 on Amazon
item.itunes:title: The Fanttik S1 Pro electric screwdriver with three torque settings drops to $40 on Amazon
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Opening a laptop or building a new PC usually involves a lot of tedious twisting with a manual screwdriver, which can be a real drag when you've got dozens of tiny fasteners to deal with. A powered driver with adjustable torque takes some of that work off your hands, and that's where the Fanttik S1 Pro Electric Screwdriver comes in, and it's currently on sale on Amazon for its lowest prive yet.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover
Fanttik S1 Pro Electric Screwdriver
Brand
Fanttik
Battery Capacity
2000mAh lithium-ion, 3.7V
Tool Type
Screwdriver
Cordless?
Yes

The Fanttik S1 Pro is a cordless electric screwdriver that ships with 16 magnetic S2 steel bits in an aluminum alloy storage case. It has three torque settings of 1.5, 3 and 4.2 N.m, a maximum hard torque of 6 N.m, a 220 rpm motor and a 2000mAh USB-C rechargeable battery.

See at Amazon

A lot of bench-friendly features for the money

Three torque levels for small fasteners

Credit: Fanttik

The Fanttik S1 Pro has three power torque levels, aimed for specific jobs. You can, for example, use the lowest setting on small gadget screws and step up the torque for larger screws on a PC case.

This is, in short, aimed at people who regularly do fiddly work. If you build or upgrade PCs, repair phones and laptops, or tinker with small electronics, the torque settings and work light cover the basics of that job. This is perfect for building a PC because of how often you'll switch between the sizes and lengths of screws, so you can switch torque speeds very easily. Fanttik lists the speed at 220 RPM, a measured pace that fits small screws better than heavy fastening.

But the Fanttik S1 Pro doesn't just include the screwdriver; you also get 16 steel bits and a carrying case, so you don't have to try to find the right bit for the job.

There are a couple of caveats. At about 845 g, the S1 Pro is worth keeping in mind for long sessions of fine work. Also, you can't use the screwdriver while it's plugged in, so charge it before you start a long tear down or build.

At $39.99, the Fanttik S1 Pro is a solid pick for anyone who regularly opens laptops, builds PCs or repairs gadgets.. If you've been eyeing a powered driver for the bench, we think it's an easy pick-up before Amazon's early Black Friday deals wrap up.

item.title: Windows once ran the world's 10th-fastest supercomputer, and now even Microsoft's supercomputers run Linux
item.itunes:title: Windows once ran the world's 10th-fastest supercomputer, and now even Microsoft's supercomputers run Linux
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Almost two decades ago, in November of 2008, the Dawning 5000A at the Shanghai Supercomputer Center was considered the tenth-fastest supercomputer in the world... and it ran Windows. It packed 30,720 AMD Opteron cores while achieving 180.6 teraflops on the Linpack benchmark, carrying a Windows HPC 2008 label on the TOP500 supercomputer list. That was the highest a Windows system had ever achieved, and none have come close since then.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Today, all 500 systems on the TOP500 run Linux, and that's been the case since November 2017. Even Microsoft has thrown in the towel on that front, with Azure's Eagle claiming the third spot in 2023 running Ubuntu 22.04. This is a pretty amusing situation for the company that once called Linux "a cancer" to find itself in.

Microsoft's attempts at a Windows-based supercomputer were serious, too. It all started with one engineer who decided to write to Bill Gates, and snowballed into a dedicated version of Windows that could produce results competitive with Linux. However, Microsoft was seven years behind Linux on the TOP500 list, helped in part by a Unix lawsuit that had nothing to do with Microsoft.

Linux was on the TOP500 years before Windows

And an AT&T lawsuit helped it get there

Avalon, a cluster at Los Alamos National Laboratory built from 68 DEC Alpha processors connected over ordinary Fast Ethernet, was the first Linux machine to break into the TOP500. It reached #314 in June 1998 with 19.33 gigaflops, and Michael Warren, its project manager, explained why Linux made it possible. "Linux can be obtained at no cost through the Internet, but that is minor compared to its other advantages." One of the more important aspects, he said, was that "we can go to the source code and fix many problems immediately."

Avalon was a Beowulf cluster, a design developed at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center a few years earlier. Donald Becker and Thomas Sterling began working on it in late 1993, building a prototype in early 1994 from 16 DX4 processors connected by Ethernet, using off-the-shelf hardware. However, Linux wasn't Sterling's first choice.

When asked about the project, Sterling said the following in a Q&A with OpenHPC in 2016: "Berkeley Software stack, which was funded by DARPA, was being litigated against by AT&T," he said. "At that time, my team and I were supported by NASA, and NASA would not allow us to use BSD which we otherwise would have for our experiments in scientific cluster computing."

The litigation Sterling is referring to was the case that AT&T brought against Berkely over its usage of Unix code, which ran from April 1992 until a settlement in February 1994. Even though a cleaned-up BSD release arrived a few months later, Beowulf's development had already started. BSD wasn't an option for NASA, and Beowulf used Linux, so Avalon followed its design.

When Microsoft took interest in the high performance computing space, Linux's dominance was already apparent. It had passed Unix on the TOP500 by June 2004 with 291 systems, whereas Unix had 182, and by November 2005 Linux was on 372 of the 500. Windows, at the time, could only be found on one.

Microsoft's push came from an engineer going to Bill Gates

Gates took it seriously

Kyril Faenov joined Microsoft in 1998 after Valence Research had been acquired by Microsoft, which was a server clustering startup he had co-founded. A few years after joining the company, he wrote to Bill Gates urging Microsoft to enter high-performance computing, and he later formed the company's HPC group in 2004.

On November 15 in 2005, Gates held a keynote at SC05 in Seattle, pitching the idea that one day, supercomputers could be affordable enough for individual departments to own. "What we see as a key trend here is that we will have supercomputers of all sizes, including ones that will cost less than $10,000 and be able to sit at your desk or in a department," he said. He was candid about Microsoft's motives, too, telling InformationWeek that week that "we got into technical computing because it's a big enough field for us, in terms of the software opportunity, to justify that alone."

Microsoft's timing confused some analysts. John Abbot of The 451 Group told Computerworld that he found it "astonishing how they missed out on this altogether." There was just one Windows system in the TOP500, a Dell cluster at the Cornell Theory Center in 311th place, and Cornell had been putting Windows clusters on the list since 2001. One machine had reached No. 49 in June 2003, years before Microsoft had a dedicated HPC product.

Microsoft's dedicated HPC product arrived in June 2006 as Windows Compute Cluster Server 2003, at an estimated $469 per node. It included a job scheduler and MS-MPI, based on Argonne National Laboratory's open-source MPICH2, to coordinate work and communication across a cluster. Bob Muglia, senior vice president of Microsoft's Server and Tools Business, said the company wanted HPC to be "as easy to locate and use as printers are today." Microsoft's own Rainier cluster reached No. 106 on the TOP500 in June 2007.

Windows peaked at No. 10 in November 2008

It never had more than four systems on the list

Microsoft's first big result came at ISC in June of 2008, when the National Center for Supercomputing Applications ran a beta of Windows HPC Server 2008 on its Abe cluster and hit 68.5 teraflops across 9,472 cores. Microsoft announced it as No. 23 on the list, and Faenov said it showed "Windows can scale to the rarefied atmosphere of the top 25 supercomputing systems in the world." It was released that following September at $475 per node, alongside Cray's $25,000 CX1, which was as close as anyone got to the desk-sized supercomputer Gates had envisioned.

Then, in November of 2008, the Dawning 5000A in Shanghai reached #10 in November 2008, becoming what TOP500 called "the most powerful system outside the U.S." and "the largest system which can be operated with Windows HPC 2008 operating system." As noted by InfoWorld at the time, just a year earlier "the best Microsoft could do was 116th place." Looking through TOP500's current database places Dawning at #11 as it includes an additional Kraken XT5 entry, but the original November 2008 results ranked it tenth.

In a broader sense, though, the numbers were never all that good. At any given time, Windows never had more than four systems on any edition of the TOP500, and IDC stated that Microsoft owned less than 5% of HPC server revenue, compared to 74% for Linux and just over 21% for Unix. Timothy Prickett Morgan of The Register stated that "At $475 a pop, Microsoft has to sell the operating system on 2.1 million server nodes to make $1 billion. The world only consumes a little more than 8 million servers a year."

Microsoft still had successes, though. At SC10 in November of 2010, Microsoft announced that Windows HPC Server had passed a petaflop on TSUBAME 2.0 at the Tokyo Institute of Technology. "It broke the Petaflop barrier and was on par with Linux at this scale," said Satoshi Matsuoka, lead of TSUBAME. Only seven supercomputers had manage to achieve a petaflop of compute at that point, according to Network World, putting the Windows result in top-10 territory.

Unfortunately for Microsoft, TSUBAME 2.0 later took #4... as a Linux system. The team had run Linpack on both operating systems, and Bill Hilf, then general manager of Microsoft's Technical Computing group, told Network World that the results were less than 5% apart. Linux came out ahead because it ran on slightly more nodes, and TOP500 only accepts one result per machine. Abe's entry is even stranger: its 68.48-teraflop result matches the Windows run Microsoft announced, and the system name includes both operating systems, but TOP500 records it as Linux too. What this means, though, is that two of the best results ever produced by Windows aren't counted as Windows in the TOP500 rankings.

Hilf at the time said that "we're not trying to beat Linux." He then went on to say that "we're not trying to be a supercomputing company. We're trying to say 'how do we mainstream all of this stuff so that HPC becomes broadly available at all levels.'" He stated instead that their focus was on "the bottom 500,000 computing users."

To be fair to Microsoft, the company had been heading in that direction for quite a while. With the release of Windows HPC Server 2008 R2 in that September, HPC Services for Excel 2010 was able to offload spreadsheet calculations to a cluster, and Microsoft was also working on integrating Azure. Microsoft claimed that its performance was equal to Linux at 32% to 51% lower costs over five years. At this point, the company was targeting businesses that already used Windows and needed more computing power, rather than the top of the TOP500.

Microsoft moved HPC into Azure and stopped selling a supercomputer OS

HPC Pack became a free add-on

In 2010, Microsoft launched a Technical Computing initiative, which Faenov had argued in favour of to Steve Ballmer's office, making the cloud a central component of its plans. In July 2011, Faenov moved into an advisory role reporting to Satya Nadella, then president of Server and Tools, while the HPC business was folded into the Server and Cloud Division under Ryan Waite. HPCwire's analysis concluded that it was "clear Microsoft is looking to Azure as a way to re-energize its HPC business."

Microsoft's deciated supercomputing edition ended in December 2012 with HPC Pack 2012. Microsoft at the time said that "Unlike previous releases, there is no longer a HPC SKU for Windows Server 2012. Instead, we are releasing this as a free add-on pack." Just six years after Compute Cluster Server was priced at $469 per node, the cluster software became free to use with regular Windows Server.

For a number of years, the Dawning 5000A remained on the TOP500, dropping to #436 in June 2015. This was the last Windows system recorded on the list, and there have been none since then.

That same June, Jan Wender of German IT services firm, "science+computing" was asked by insideHPC why he felt that Windows HPC had never caught on. "There has been no clear performance benefit from using Windows HPC," was his answer. After all, academic research software was built with the expectation of running on Unix-like systems for decades, and engineering software originally developed for Unix had already been ported to Linux. In his experience, Windows HPC was mostly found in "smaller installations with rather specific applications only available on Windows (and then sometimes not even using the HPC pack)."

Microsoft's Windows HPC software is still around today, though its days are numbered. The company announced that it was retiring HPC Pack in August 2026, and HPC Pack 2019's support is ending in August 2027. HPC Pack 2016 is also set to be retired in January 2027. Microsoft still supports existing deployments for now, but its dedicated HPC software is nearing the end of the road.

Microsoft's last Windows supercomputer was named after the man who started it

A quiet tribute to Kyril Faenov

In November 2012, a new Microsoft system appeared on the TOP500 at #165, a virtual cluster on Azure. It packed 8,064 cores on HP servers connected by InfiniBand, running Windows Server 2012 in Hyper-V virtual machines. It hit 151.3 teraflops at 90.2% efficiency, which Hilf presented as proof that Azure could handle what Microsoft called "Big Compute." TOP500 lists its operating system as "Windows Azure," and it was the last Windows system put on the list by Microsoft itself.

It was called Faenov. Microsoft never gave a reason for the name, and Hilf's own announcement didn't either. However, it's pretty clear that this is an homage to Kyril Faenov, the man who lead Microsoft's HPC efforts.

Faenov grew up in Moscow, training with the Olympic reserve swimming team and studying physics and mathematics. His colleagues spoke highly of his dedicated to Microsoft's HPC efforts, and it seems unlikely that Microsoft's HPC division would not have existed without him. Hilf recalled that "He would frequently say, 'I get out of bed because I know if we're successful here, it will change the world for my daughters in the future."

By 2012, Faenov had moved on to become general manager of SQL Test, but he passed away in May that year, aged 38.

Microsoft's supercomputers run Linux now

Eagle runs Ubuntu

Windows may not be in the TOP500, but Microsoft certainly is. Azure's Eagle entered at #3 in November 2023 with 561.2 petaflops on Nvidia H100 GPUs, and it remains at No. 7 on the June 2026 list. It runs Ubuntu 22.04, and Microsoft's other entries all run Ubuntu too.

Microsoft's shift to Linux had already been visible for years, with the company saying that a deal to acquire Cycle Computing would "further enhance our support of Linux HPC workloads." That November, the last two non-Linux systems on the TOP500, a pair of IBM POWER7 machines running AIX at the China Meteorological Administration, moved off the list. Since then, every system has been classified as Linux.

What "Linux" means on that list isn't necessarily what you or I would think of, though. For example, IBM's own Blue Gene/Q machines are counted as Linux despite their compute nodes running CNK, a lightweight kernel that can't even fork() a process, and full Linux only runs on the I/O nodes. Fugaku, led by Satoshi Matsuoka, pairs Red Hat Enterprise Linux with McKernel, El Capitan runs LLNL's Red Hat-based TOSS, and the current #1, China's LineShine, runs Kylin OS.

Despite the fact that Windows never really saw success in the HPC space, Microsoft has some of the fastest supercomputers in the world. They just don't run Windows.

item.itunes:summary:
Vibe coding is changing how software gets built, allowing developers to turn ideas into working applications with the help of AI. Some of these projects are already moving beyond simple experiments and starting to challenge established software. From familiar desktop applications to surprisingly feature-rich productivity tools, these alternatives offer capabilities you'd normally expect from commercial products. I explored four projects that demonstrate how AI-assisted development is creating practical alternatives to the software we use every day.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

WordCraft

A lightweight word processor with a familiar workflow

If you've spent years using Microsoft Word, switching to another word processor can feel like an unnecessary learning curve. WordCraft takes a different approach. Built in Rust, this open-source editor brings a ribbon-based interface into a lightweight, modern application.

The ribbon-based layout makes the editor easy to navigate, particularly if you're accustomed to Microsoft Word. Common formatting options are readily accessible, so switching doesn't involve much of a learning curve. There's quite a bit packed into the editor, too: document styles, tables, track changes, references, and even mail merge. DOCX support is another welcome addition, allowing you to work with existing Microsoft Word documents without starting from scratch.

WordCraft isn't limited to desktop use. It runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux, and can even work in a browser through WebAssembly. Its source code is publicly available, giving developers the opportunity to explore and contribute to the project.

WordCraft

WordCraft is a free, open-source word processor built in pure Rust by the ArtCraft team.

See at Github

OpenTodo

A task manager that helps you plan your day

A long task list doesn't necessarily translate into a productive day. OpenTodo addresses this gap by combining task management with tools that help you organize your time. It's a local-first alternative to Todoist that puts more emphasis on organizing your workload than simply keeping track of pending tasks.

Natural-language input is one of the features I found particularly convenient. For instance, typing "Call Sarah next Wednesday at 3 PM #work p1" automatically identifies the due date, time, project, and priority. It saves you from having to fill in each detail separately. Once tasks are added, lists, boards, and timeline views offer different ways to organize your workload.

OpenTodo also brings several planning tools into the same workspace. There's a calendar for time-blocking, along with recurring tasks, reminders, habits, and time tracking. CalDAV support is particularly useful if you already rely on an external calendar and don't want to maintain two separate schedules.

I can see this approach working well when personal tasks and professional responsibilities compete for space on the same day. Instead of simply reminding you what needs to get done, it helps you organize when and how to tackle those tasks.

OpenTodo

OpenTodo is an open-source, local-first, self-hosted task and project manager designed as a privacy-focused alternative to commercial apps like Todoist.

See at Github
I started using VS Code with this new-age AI-coding tool, and now I can't go back

The coding setup I always wanted.

2
By  Parth Shah

PhotoCraft

An ambitious alternative to Photoshop

Photoshop's extensive editing capabilities are impressive, but not everyone needs to rely on Adobe's software for image manipulation. PhotoCraft is a vibe-coded image editor that aims to deliver a capable editing experience without the commercial software overhead.

Layers form the foundation of PhotoCraft's editing environment, making it approachable for anyone who has used image-editing software before. Adjustment layers, masks, layer styles, vector shapes, text, and brushes are all part of the toolkit. I was particularly interested in its support for layered PSD files, as it means existing compositions don't necessarily have to be flattened before moving between applications.

What sets PhotoCraft apart is its command-based architecture. Alongside conventional editing controls, operations can be triggered through a command-line interface or even through AI agents. That opens up possibilities beyond the usual point-and-click editing workflow.

The project is still in early alpha, so I wouldn't rely on it for critical professional work just yet. Still, the combination of traditional editing features and command-based controls makes PhotoCraft an ambitious project worth keeping an eye on.

PhotoCraft

PhotoCraft is a free, open-source, and offline image editor written from scratch in pure Rust as a clean-room reimplementation of Adobe Photoshop.

See at PhotoCraft

PDFCraft

A simpler way to handle everyday PDF tasks

You don't always need a full-fledged PDF editor to get work done. Sometimes, merging a few documents, extracting pages, or reducing a file's size is all you want. PDFCraft focuses on these everyday operations, providing an open-source alternative to heavyweight PDF applications like Adobe Acrobat.

The app covers the essentials: merging and splitting documents, compressing files, rotating pages, rearranging content, and extracting individual pages. There's support for adding watermarks, converting images into PDFs, and managing document metadata, too.

PDFCraft keeps its common operations easy to find, so there's little need to dig through complicated menus for routine tasks. This is particularly handy when you need to process several documents in succession. If your requirements rarely extend beyond preparing invoices, organizing reports, or making quick adjustments, this may be all you need.

PDFCraft

PDFCraft is a free, open-source PDF reader, editor, and document workbench built natively in Rust.

See at Github
I tried replacing Microsoft 365 with a vibe-coded app and a popular FOSS toolkit, and only one stuck

I went looking for something new and ended up sticking with a familiar approach to productivity.

7
By  Yash Patel

Sometimes, the best upgrade is a different tool

You don't have to replace your entire software stack to improve your workflow. A small tool that solves one specific problem can sometimes make a noticeable difference. These projects are worth exploring, even if you aren't ready to abandon your trusted applications. I'd rather experiment with something that genuinely improves how I work than stick with the same software simply because I've used it for years.

item.title: I connected my Shield TV Pro's Plex server to lossless CD rips, and its companion app made them portable
item.itunes:title: I connected my Shield TV Pro's Plex server to lossless CD rips, and its companion app made them portable
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I finally added a proper NAS to my home network and mounted it to my Nvidia Shield TV Pro for Plex server access. I wanted Jellyfin and Plex to access my centralized media library. Namely, my lossless CD rips I've been working on. After that, I decided to try the Plex music companion app for remote access to my self-hosted Spotify on the go.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

It wasn't hard to set up, but it took several steps to get everything configured correctly. Previously, I was using connected USB drives and an old server I resurrected as my network storage. Once I had my CD rips organized on my NAS and mounted on my Shield TV Pro, firing up Plexamp to listen to quality audio was a cinch.

Migrating lossless CD rips from external USB drives to my NAS

It was an easy process

After going through stacks of CDs and perfecting my ripping workflow, I wanted to consolidate my lossless rips, so I got a NAS to store them. My ripped FLAC files had been scattered across a sea of internal and external drives. Once I transferred them to my NAS, I mounted it on my Plex server on my Nvidia Shield TV Pro. The most time-consuming part was adding them to the storage appliance. I transferred some over my network and others by connecting exFAT drives directly to it for faster transfers.

Everything was set up correctly; cover art and metadata were correct, except for a few missing album covers on some rare albums. I mounted my NAS on my Shield TV Pro so the Plex server could access and stream my files to my devices. Once that was complete, I added the libraries to my media folders via Plex Web and tested them out on my TV.

I confirmed the server could read and stream the CD rips, then removed the existing USB drives from the libraries via Plex Web. Then unplugged the USB drives from the Shield TV Pro to clean up the cables and clutter under my television. The files were on my NAS, the drives and cables were cleaned up, and the final touches on my music library were mostly complete. I was ready to add the music companion to the equation.

My Nvidia Shield TV Pro is old, but newer streaming boxes should still steal its best features

It's seven years old, but still has some quality features new boxes need.

7
By  Brian Burgess

Plexamp worked with CD rips straightaway

It was a matter of installation and use

To take the music from my Plex server on my Shield TV Pro portable, I installed Plexamp on my iPhone and Google Pixel for testing. Once I installed it, I signed in to my Plex account, and my music collection populated the app right away. Artists and albums displayed on my phones, and I tested a few songs, playback controls, and switching to make sure my music library worked.

Once that was done, I went out to run errands around town and listened to my quality CD files like it was a music streaming service. While I was mobile, I could flip between tracks, albums, and artists, and control playback as I could at home on Wi-Fi or using a streaming service like Spotify or Apple Music. The interface is intuitive and easy to use to navigate my collection in the car or while in stores.

I built a self-hosted music streaming service with my NAS and Plex

Using a storage appliance and free tools from Plex

Building my own self-hosted Spotify-like service with my CD rips, Shield TV Pro, NAS, and Plex was more straightforward than setting it up with Jellyfin. That is, until the Jellybox app and its Relay server Plugin were added to the project recently. Its configuration lets me listen to my quality lossless music files at home and take them with me on the go without port forwarding or downloads.

However, Plex does the same thing and doesn't require a plugin to configure. I only needed to organize my storage and music, install Plexamp on my device, and sign in to my account. While remote video playback requires Plex Pass, the remote music streaming functionality has been free for the past few years. With a subscription, you get additional features like offline downloads, advanced mixing, and music discovery. But the core ability to listen to my music from my server is free.

4 Plex companion apps that take my media server to the next level

These often overlooked apps will improve your Plex experience.

8
By  Brian Burgess

Consolidating my CD rips to my NAS and making them portable with Plex

It is much easier to manage my lossless CD rips on my NAS than across multiple USB drives connected to my Shield TV Pro's Plex server. My music lives on one storage device, and I can rip new CDs directly to it. It's also easier for manual library management and produces fewer duplicate metadata files.

In my experience, sometimes the music stops while I'm remote. My music stream with Plexamp drops less than Jellybox and its encrypted Jellyfin Relay plugin, but more than streaming services. Still, I would rather listen to better audio quality for music I own than pay to stream.

Plexamp

item.itunes:title: I run a 2B vision model on my phone and stopped sending my screenshots to ChatGPT and Claude
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Screenshots have become one of the main ways people use AI. Ever since the big players, Gemini in particular, introduced the ability to upload images and analyze them, it's become a staple in the workflow. I know it is for me, at least. There's nothing more convenient than snapping something and just showing it to an AI, as opposed to taking notes and describing what you saw to your chatbot. And that extends to mobile.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

The problem is that the screenshots, or any file for that matter, that you upload to a chatbot are subject to each provider's retention and training policies, for anywhere from a couple of days to a couple of years, depending on whether or not you opted in to model training. That's not something you want for screenshots that contain personal information. Local models have had the ability to analyze images not long after the cloud ones, but it only really became more popular around 2025-2026, and I've definitely been taking advantage of it.

My local LLM didn't replace my $20 Claude subscription, it replaced everything I was never comfortable sending to the cloud

There are many things Qwen3.6 struggles with, but keeping my data safe isn't one of them

10
By  Abhinav Raj

What actually leaves your phone with a screenshot

Every detail in the shot goes along with your prompt

Vision models have gotten very good at reading text out of images, down to the name on a notification banner that popped up right as you snapped it. That means sending a screenshot to a chatbot is basically the same as pasting every word on that screen into the chat, whether you noticed it was there or not. Whatever gets uploaded then sits under that company's data policy. OpenAI may use chats from consumer plans to improve models, unless you turn off "improve model for everyone", and Anthropic can hold onto chats for up to five years for model improvement if you opted into training. item.title: KVM-over-IP gave me an office workstation that actually works from anywhere
item.itunes:title: KVM-over-IP gave me an office workstation that actually works from anywhere
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Remote access for your desktop PC is often solved by using a VPN or remote desktop software. That's how I've managed things for years: a combination of remote desktop software and Tailscale, so the software only worked on my tailnet. It was smooth, secure, and worked everywhere, until one day Windows rebooted after an update when I wasn't at home and didn't make it back to the desktop.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

But it didn't have to be like this. I'm already familiar with KVM-over-IP devices, as I run them in my home lab. I've even used one to remotely overclock my PC from BIOS, but I never thought about keeping it plugged in because I had software solutions for remote access. So I plugged it back in, and now my desktop workstation is reachable from anywhere I am.

I ditched physical monitors for KVM-over-IP, and my server closet actually looks clean now

I always hated the extra clutter

11
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Remote desktop software stops working exactly when I need it

RDP, Parsec, and Sunshine all depend on Windows being up and logged in

I've used many remote desktop tools over the years, and I can't argue against how useful they are. Being able to remote into your powerful desktop from anywhere and run programs as if you're sitting at your desk at home is fantastic. But it has one major issue: all software-based solutions live inside your OS. That's fine if nothing goes wrong, but a failed update, a BitLocker issue, or anything that keeps you from the desktop environment can stop you from accessing your PC.

The answer is a small box that plugs into your PC and your network. An IP KVM is essentially a virtual keyboard and mouse you can control over the network, with HDMI capture so you can see what's going on. Your PC just sees it as a monitor and input devices, and you don't need to install anything on the host PC to use it.

This remote desktop tool finally replaced RDP and VNC in my home lab

RustDesk is a remote desktop tool that left RDP and VNC in the dust in my home lab.

5
By  Abhishek Kumar Mishra

You used to need server hardware for this

IPMI-style control arrived for ordinary desktops, and the hardware is tiny

The ability to control your computer remotely from KVM-over-IP used to be limited to server hardware, or to a few specialized motherboards with IPMI control. I hunted for weeks for a PCIe IPMI card for the Asus motherboard in my server and ended up buying a motherboard with a mangled CPU socket to get the expansion card I needed.

But that PCIe card only works on a handful of Asus motherboards. What works on any computer is PiKVM, which was the open-source original that started a new product category. Now we have options from JetKVM, NanoKVM, and GL.iNet, and all of my current KVM-over-IP devices are from GL.iNet.

While the multi-device box I use has PoE, I use it with a USB-C wall adapter instead. I've got a whole-house UPS, so I'm not worried about power, and then I can use the KVM-over-IP box on any of my network switches. The rest of it is simple. HDMI out from the GPU (this can be the onboard graphics), and one USB between the back of the PC and the KVM. Capture tops out at either 1080p60 or 4K30, depending on the device, so if you're using a high-refresh-rate monitor like me, you'll want to use a second GPU output for the KVM.

Power control is essential

While the device can control my PC during boot or in the BIOS, it still has one restriction. It can't press the power button. Okay, it can use Wake-on-LAN to wake the PC from sleep, trigger a Fingerbot to turn it on, or use an ATX board that splices into the front-panel headers to turn it on.

My fallback is a smart plug and a "restore on AC power" setting in the BIOS. Cycling the plug from Home Assistant takes seconds, and then the BIOS setting should work. It's not perfect, but the ATX board does the work most of the time.

Remote access feels like the “final boss” of running a home lab, but NetBird made it a few clicks

Accessing your lab away from home shouldn't be complicated

1
By  Ty Sherback

Tailscale is what makes it work from anywhere

The KVM joins the tailnet, so nothing is exposed and nothing is forwarded

GL.iNet used to offer only OpenVPN and WireGuard for secure remote access, but now you can use Tailscale. After adding the KVM to my tailnet, I don't really have to think about it anymore. It might look like the same software issue that pushed me to use a KVM in the first place, but the GL.iNet box has no power button, never sleeps, and is connected to a giant UPS. If the KVM is offline, I have bigger issues than remote access.

And it's pretty responsive. I've used it to remotely overclock my PC from the BIOS, and it felt as smooth as when sitting at my desk. Typing has a little bit of lag, as does the mouse cursor, but no more than typing in cloud-based text editors. There's also a vendor-based cloud relay if I'm on a device that's not on my tailnet, Goodcloud, but I only use that if I'm using something I don't want to add to Tailscale, like a PC I don't own.

I still use Remote Desktop for some tasks

For longer work sessions, I still prefer remote desktop apps like RustDesk. They're sharper and smoother than using the KVM-over-IP route. The KVM is there to ensure I can reach my workstation if it's turned off, or stuck on reboot, or any of the other things that can go wrong with Windows and put me offline. The KVM is good enough for short tasks, but I'd rather keep it to those.

I was ready to pay for a remote desktop app, but Windows 11 already ships one for free

You won't see Microsoft advertise this one, though

5
By  Abhinav Raj

An IP KVM is a keyboard plugged into your PC that lives on the network

You want to trust the company that makes it

There's a good reason I use Tailscale for my IP KVM, with ACLs to limit which devices can access it. In March 2026, security researchers found nine vulnerabilities in popular IP KVMs. These ranged from missing brute-force protection and firmware update verification to other issues. Then there's the NanoKVM's onboard microphone, which is worrying, but if someone has device control of your IP KVM, you have more to worry about than it listening to you. It still requires root access to your device.

PiKVM was overkill until I realized what else it could do

I built my PiKVM for emergencies, but it’s quickly turned into the tool that keeps my server and my patience from falling apart.

By  Jeff Butts

Now my workstation is reachable whether Windows is running or not

Most remote access tools only work when your computer is on and logged in. That's not always the situation, especially with desktop workstations, and even then you can't do some tasks like change BIOS settings. A KVM-over-IP device is the always-on solution that lets you access your computer securely from anywhere.

GL.iNet Comet X

The GL.iNet Comet X is a KVM-over-IP device that supports up to four devices, letting you use and manage them from anywhere with an internet connection.

item.title: Your AMD GPU might be burning through your SSD's remaining lifespan - here's how to check
item.itunes:title: Your AMD GPU might be burning through your SSD's remaining lifespan - here's how to check
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If you have a Radeon GPU in your system, there's a pretty nasty bug in some versions of the driver that puts a never-ending load on your storage, and you could be affected. A background process has been discovered writing to the system drive around the clock, even while the PC is completely idle, and AMD has confirmed the behavior. Your card itself isn't at fault and the fix is as simple as updating your driver, but it's still not in the driver branch most people are using.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover
Windows 11's default settings are quietly wearing out your SSD and turning them off can extend its life

A couple of tweaks can quietly extend the remaining lifespan of your drive

5
By  Anmol Mehrotra

What AMD's driver is actually doing to your SSD

It affects some systems more than others

When you install AMD's GPU driver, by default it will also come with the Adrenalin software suite, where you're able to change things about the card and how it functions. With this software comes a Windows service called AMD External Events Utility, which runs in the background and handles things like hotkeys and detecting new displays. Normally, you'd never need to know this service exists, but it seems to be malfunctioning in a way that completely hammers your system drive with writes.

A forum member on ComputerBase named Necandi traced its activity using Windows’ built-in event tracing, and they found that atieclxx.exe was copying its own executable out of the driver folder and into the Windows system profile every second, all day, no matter what the PC was doing. A company representative on Reddit gave AMD’s explanation, and they say the problem comes from an interaction between the External Events Utility and Microsoft’s PCIe filter driver.

Reports generally point to Adrenalin versions 26.10.1 and 26.10.2 being the affected versions, although some users believe the behavior could exist in prior versions of the driver. Some Radeon owners say they don't see any unusual disk activity at all, so it really varies system to system.

5 ways the Nvidia app falls behind AMD Adrenalin

AMD's GPU software is full of handy features.

2
By  Joe Rice-Jones

A few megabytes a second adds up fast

SSDs aren't made to last forever

Hard drives can handle this sort of constant writing behavior a bit better than SSDs can as far as endurance goes, but most people house their OS on an SSD these days, and solid state storage can only be written to a limited number of times before it wears out completely. A typical 1TB SSD with TLC flash has around 600 TBW, or terabytes written. During normal use, the average user simply doesn't approach that limit through the lifetime of their system, but with a bug like this, the constant writing can add up really quickly.

User reports put the write rate anywhere from about 0.6MB/s to 5MB/s. In my experience, it hovered around 0.6MB/s before I simply stopped the service from activating. At that rate, that's about 52GB a day and about 20TB for a year, which still isn't terrible, but at the high end of 5MB/s, that's about 432GB a day, which would use up a quarter of that same drive's rating every year.

To check if you're affected, open Task Manager and then sort by Disk usage. Brief blips of write activity are normal, but if you're seeing the "atieclxx.exe" process continually writing to disk, your system has the bug.

If you boot Proxmox from an SSD, disable these two services to prevent wearing out your drive

A couple of optimizations to help your Proxmox SSD stay in tip-top shape

19
By  Ayush Pande

AMD has delivered a fix

Well, sort of

The good news is, AMD has already supplied a fix for this in the latest Adrenalin driver at the time of writing. The bad news is it's contained in an optional driver download, and Adrenalin doesn't tell you that.

If I go to update my drivers in Adrenalin right now, it says my 26.10.1 driver is the latest. The fix is in Adrenalin 26.11.1, released on November 12, and the release notes list fixes for both the excessive writes at idle and the extra writes when moving or resizing windows. By default, AMD puts users on the "Recommended" driver updates, and changing it involves going into the AMD Install Manager and selecting "Recommended + Optional". I assume the fix will be coming to a driver in the recommended branch very soon, if it hasn't already by the time this article goes live.

If you're affected by this bug, that would be my first course of action. Choose the optional driver branch if you're on one of the affected versions, even if you don't see excessive disk usage in Task Manager. It's not entirely clear when or how this behavior is triggered, so even if it seems like you're good now, a few percent off of your SSD's health simply isn't worth the risk.

All the settings in AMD, Intel, and Nvidia's drivers you need to enable

Optimized defaults get your PC booting but there are tweaks to do for every GPU maker

2
By  Joe Rice-Jones

A bug that's annoying at best and potentially damaging at worst

For a lot of Radeon owners, this caused maybe a couple percent of their SSD's rated endurance, and that's definitely annoying but not catastrophic. It won't go down in history alongside something like the Intel 13th and 14th Gen disaster, but it's certainly something to keep an eye on if you run an AMD GPU. The fix is simple: update your drivers and keep an eye on SSD health.

item.title: Someone built a gadget that lets the Dreamcast play N64 games, and it's absolutely wild
item.itunes:title: Someone built a gadget that lets the Dreamcast play N64 games, and it's absolutely wild
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Dreamcart lets the Dreamcast boot N64 cartridges through a combination of hardware and emulation.
  • The build requires a Dreamcast, a donor N64, cartridges, dcload-ip disc, CMSIS-DAP probe, SDKs and OpenOCD.
  • Dreamcart also supports SNES/Genesis carts or ROMs; VMU emulates 66-block Save Pak (32 KB) so saves work.

If this wild gadget existed in the early 2000s, it could have single-handedly ended the console wars. Okay, probably not — but it's still pretty cool. Modder Throaty Mumbo's latest project, the Dreamcart, is an adapter that plugs into the Dreamcast's controller, allowing it to boot N64 cartridges through emulation (via Time Extension).

To make your own, you need a Dreamcast and a donor N64 console and, of course, Nintendo 64 cartridges. On top of that, you need dcload-ip burned to a disc and a CMSIS-DAP debug probe (a Rapsberry Pi Debug Probe would work) to handle loading the console's firmware. You'll also need the Raspberry Pi Pico SDK, OpenOCD, KallistiOS, and dc-tool-ip.

Only a handful of games are confirmed to be compatible

Dreamcart also works with SNES and Sega Genesis cartridges

The entire process seems pretty complicated, especially when you can just play the games directly on an N64. But what's the fun in that, right? Games that are confirmed to be compatible include the following: Super Mario 64, Mario Kart 64, Kirby 64, Rayman 2, Cruis'n USA, Cruis'n World, Elmo's Number Journey, THPS 2, Pokémon Stadium 2, and Donkey Kong 64. Throaty Mumbo has a full video of the build process up on his YouTube channel (check out the video above). Steps to build the Dreamcart are up on their GitHub page, too.

On the project's GitHub page, Throaty Mumbo mentions that it's likely you could just use ROMs and not physical cartridges with the setup they've created, but they say that "using actual cartridges is cooler." The mod also works with SNES and Sega Genesis cartridges, as long as you can get your hands on both 16-bit consoles' cart readers.

Interestingly, even saving with games that record a Memory Card works because the Dreamcast's VMU emulates the Save Pak using 66 blocks, which takes up just 32kb. In other N64-related news, a fan-made, AI-assisted port of Halo called Halo: Dreamcast Evolved recently released (yes, you read that correctly).

I played the Switch 2 Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on PC without an emulator, and it runs shockingly well

It runs almost as good as it does on the Switch 2 (and even better sometimes).

By  Patrick O'Rourke
